findings.situation: A filer signed a purchase contract for the vehicle before January 20, 2025 but took delivery or title after January 19, 2025, so the acquisition date could be read as either the contract date or the delivery date.
findings.source_text: i4562 (2025) p. 13, Line 25: "certain qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025, and certain qualified property acquired after September 27, 2017, and before January 20, 2025"
findings.why: Neither the text nor the question's help says which date counts as 'acquire'. A filer who goes by delivery answers yes and gets 100%, while one who goes by the binding contract date answers no and gets 40%. The 100% allowance generally treats property under a written binding contract signed before January 20, 2025 as acquired before that date.

findings.situation: A filer whose vehicle is used 50% or less for business (or must use ADS, or was disposed of in 2025) honestly answers 'full' because they believe they claimed the allowance, and the lines then compute a 100% or 40% special allowance.
findings.source_text: i4562 p. 7, Exceptions: 'Qualified property does not include: • Listed property used 50% or less in a qualified business use ... • Any property required to be depreciated under the Alternative Depreciation System (ADS) ... • Property placed in service ... and disposed of in the same tax year'; i4562 p. 13, Section A: 'Listed property used 50% or less in a qualified business use ... does not qualify for the ... special depreciation allowance.'
findings.why: The question asks only 'did you claim the special depreciation allowance (full)'. It does not say the vehicle must be qualified property, and its help gives no guidance. Line 16 needs zero for a non-qualifying vehicle, but a 'full' answer feeds a positive allowance into bonus_2025 and line 16.

findings.situation: A filer owns an interest in a partnership or S corporation that placed 5-year property in service in 2025 and made a different election than the filer made for the vehicle, so the filer answers 'no' even though the filer's own 5-year property is treated consistently.

findings.why: The election out covers only property owned by the person making it. The phrase "all 5-year property ... that you ... placed in service" does not exclude property placed in service by a pass-through entity, whose separate election cannot make the filer's own class inconsistent.

findings.situation: Some of the filer's 2025 5-year property cannot take the special allowance at all, such as a vehicle used 50% or less for business or property that must use ADS, and the filer answers 'no' because that property got no allowance.

findings.why: A filer can read "that choice" as either the election out or simply whether the allowance was taken on each item. findings.situation: A filer claimed an alternative motor vehicle credit (or, for a vehicle placed in service before 2007, a qualified electric vehicle credit) for the vehicle and truthfully reports its full cost, reduced only by the gas guzzler tax as the question directs.

findings.why: The question names the gas guzzler tax as the only reduction and leaves out the vehicle credits. The credit amount therefore stays in the answer and inflates the business cost on line 13, the 100% cost and the unrecovered basis.

findings.situation: A filer acquired the vehicle by trading in an old car and could read 'cost' as the full purchase price, when the basis the lines need is the old car's adjusted basis plus the cash paid, or the separately tracked carryover and excess basis.

findings.why: The question says only 'cost ... or other basis' and gives no trade-in guidance, so a filer could enter the sticker price or the adjusted-basis-plus-cash figure. These give different amounts, and the trade-in adjustment for a partly-business old car makes the gap wider.

findings.situation: An employee commutes in the vehicle, and the employer either includes the value of that personal use in the employee's W-2 wages or the employee reimburses the employer for it.
findings.source_text: i4562 p. 14, Column (c): "Treat vehicles used by employees as being used 100% for business/investment purposes if the value of personal use is included in the employees' gross income, or the employees reimburse the employer for the personal use"
findings.why: The question asks "Do any of your employees use this vehicle for their own personal purposes (including commuting)?", so a truthful filer answers yes. Under the cited text, though, this vehicle counts as 100% business use, so it should not set off the 'employee_bad' gate. The question asks about personal use in general, not personal use that is neither included in income nor reimbursed.

findings.situation: A filer whose employees' personal use is included in their income reads the help sentence and is unsure whether to answer yes (because personal use happens) or no (because the vehicle is treated as 100% business).

findings.why: The help states the 100% treatment but does not say how it affects the answer. Some filers will answer yes and others no in the same situation, so the gate's value is inconsistent.

findings.situation: A filer leases a vehicle, has never used the standard mileage rate for it, deducts actual expenses, and converted it from personal to business use in 2025; they truthfully answer yes and the gate flags a prohibited method.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 6, Line 9: "You can't use actual expenses for a leased vehicle if you previously used the standard mileage rate for that vehicle"; i1040sc p. 15, Line 44b: "If you converted your vehicle during the year from personal to business use (or vice versa), enter your commuting miles only for the period you drove your vehicle for business."
findings.why: The question asks: "Did you use the standard mileage rate for this leased vehicle in an earlier year, or did you convert it during 2025 from personal use to business use or from business use to personal use?" The only bar to actual expenses on a leased vehicle is earlier use of the standard mileage rate. A 2025 conversion affects only the commuting-mile count (Line 44b) and the business-use percentage (p463 pp. 25-26), not whether actual expenses are allowed, so the 'or converted' branch makes the gate fire on permitted situations.

findings.situation: A filer who runs five or more vehicles at once, or who owns this vehicle but used actual expenses in its first year in service, prefers the standard mileage rate and answers 'standard'.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 6, Line 9: "You must use actual expenses if you used five or more vehicles simultaneously in your business (such as in fleet operations)." and "You can take the standard mileage rate for 2025 only if you: • Owned the vehicle and used the standard mileage rate for the first year you placed the vehicle in service, or • Leased the vehicle and are using the standard mileage rate for the entire lease period."

findings.situation: A filer whose business/investment use in the placed-in-service year was below 100% (for example 60%) claimed a section 179 deduction limited by line 9 (maximum × business-use percentage), and the post-recovery helper (scveh.b100) and the year-1 helper (scveh.t1s) treat that actual amount as the 100%-use figure.
findings.source_text: p946 p. 61: "Unrecovered basis is the cost or other basis ... reduced by any ... depreciation, and section 179 deductions that would have been allowable if you had used the car 100% for business and investment use and the passenger automobile limits had not applied." findings.why: Line 14 needs the section 179 amount actually claimed. The unrecovered-basis computation in b100 and t1s needs the section 179 amount that would have been allowable at 100% use without the automobile limits. Any truck or van placed in service after July 6, 2003, that is a qualified nonpersonal use vehicle." Also i4562 p. 3: "Listed property does not include: ... 4. Any truck or van placed in service after July 6, 2003, that is a qualified nonpersonal use vehicle."
findings.why: The list refuses the other excepted vehicles (transport for hire, ambulance, hearse) but leaves out qualified nonpersonal use trucks and vans. These vehicles are neither passenger automobiles nor listed property, so the passenger-automobile limits and the qualified-business-use test do not apply to them, and the gate should refuse them.

findings.situation: A vehicle whose business plus investment use was over 50% in an earlier year, but whose qualified business use that year was 50% or less, can get either answer depending on how the filer reads the two bullets.
findings.source_text: Question: "its business use was 50% or less in any earlier year" and "its qualified business use is 50% or less once you leave out uses that are not qualified business use". p463 p. 25: "You must meet this more-than-50%-use test each year of the recovery period" and "It doesn't include use for the production of income (investment use)".
findings.why: The earlier-year bullet says "business use" without the qualified-business-use exclusions. The qualified-use bullet uses the present tense "is", which reads as 2025 only. A filer could therefore count earlier-year investment or related-person use as business use and answer no, even though the text treats a year at 50% or less of qualified business use as forcing straight-line depreciation and recapture.

findings.situation: A 6,000–14,000 lb passenger-carrying vehicle has no seating behind the driver and no body section more than 30 inches ahead of the windshield, but has no integral enclosure fully enclosing the driver compartment and load carrying device; the $31,300 limit still applies, yet a truthful filer would answer no.
findings.source_text: i4562 p. 16: "That has an integral enclosure fully enclosing the driver compartment and load carrying device, does not have seating rearward of the driver's seat, and has no body section protruding more than 30 inches ahead of the leading edge of the windshield."
findings.why: The question's third exception drops the integral-enclosure requirement. That makes the exception broader, so vehicles that remain subject to the SUV limit are answered no and escape the s179_bad check.
